in_text_mentions: Diabetic cheiroarthropathy was assessed by the same examiner for the prayer sign and tabletop sign. LJM was the designation for any joint that failed to make contact (Figure 1).

panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph of both hands pressed together in a prayer position with a visible gap between the palms/fingers, illustrating the positive prayer sign described in the caption. The article is a case report of diabetic cheiroarthropathy in a patient with uncontrolled type 2 diabetes, and the caption directly labels the manifestation ('Showed positive prayer sign.'), so the panel is a real patient image showing a specific manifestation of the target disease.
panels.attribution_text: Abdalla et al. Diabetic cheiroarthropathy in uncontrolled type 2 diabetes with positive anti-nuclear antibodies: a case report from Sudan. Annals of medicine and surgery (2012) 2024. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
in_text_mentions: nderlying rheumatic disorders, particularly scleroderma and other autoimmune diseases, for example osteoarthritis. Under normal circumstances, the palmar surface of each hand can fully oppose the corresponding surface of the other hand when the hands are pressed together, resembling a prayer sign. If this action cannot be performed as seen with this patient, the sign is considered positive (Fig. 1). In addition, she was not able to lay her palms completely flat on the table at a certain spot; this indicates that there are finger flexion contractures, suggests a positive tabletop sign (Fig. 2).

panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph of the patient's hands pressed together in a prayer position with incomplete palmar apposition and visible gap between the fingers/palms, the classic positive prayer sign of diabetic cheiroarthropathy (limited joint mobility). Caption and in-text explicitly attribute this finding to diabetic cheiroarthropathy in a patient with type 1 diabetes. Skin is adequately lit and medium toned; no ethnicity or age stated.
panels.attribution_text: Boro et al. Diabetic Cheiroarthropathy in Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus and Coeliac Disease.. Cureus 2022. doi:10.7759/cureus.31708. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
in_text_mentions: s hands. He reported difficulty in carrying out fine activities like buttoning his shirt, writing, working on keyboard and injecting insulin. Hand examination showed the presence of diabetic cheiroarthropathy. This consisted of fixed flexion deformity at the level of PIP and DIP joints of both hands (Figure 1). There was thickening and induration of the skin of the palms (Figure 2). Prayer sign of the hands was positive, suggestive of limited joint mobility (Figure 3). Tinel’s and Phalen’s signs for carpal tunnel syndrome were negative. Neurological examination revealed impaired grip strength.

in_text_mentions: Diabetic cheiroarthropathy was diagnosed clinically after eliciting the “prayer” and “table top” signs. She was not able to completely lay her palms flat on a horizontal surface which denotes a positive tabletop sign.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Posteroanterior chest radiograph of the reported patient with diabetic cheiroarthropathy, showing rib crowding and chest wall deformity; the caption explicitly attributes the extraparenchymal restrictive defect to chest wall deformity in diabetic cheiroarthropathy. This is a real patient image of a manifestation of the target disease, though the chest-wall finding is not represented in the provided vocabulary, hence it is listed as a proposed finding. B: Axial HRCT of the same diabetic cheiroarthropathy patient showing normal lung parenchyma with mild anterior chest wall flattening, which the caption uses to localize the restrictive defect to the chest wall (extraparenchymal) in diabetic cheiroarthropathy. Real patient cross-sectional image supporting the disease-related chest wall deformity; the relevant finding is absent from the vocabulary, so it is recorded as a proposed finding.
